council.name: Norwich City Council
council.remit_note: Norwich City Council is a district council with city status. In Norfolk, local government is split between two councils, and Norwich does the half you meet day to day: the council housing it owns and manages itself, bin collections, parks, planning applications, and licensing — who may sell alcohol, put on entertainment, or serve hot food and drink late at night. Roads and potholes, schools and libraries, and social care for children and adults belong to Norfolk County Council instead, so you will not find those here.

topic.name: Licensing policy
topic.plain_english: The rules Norwich City Council follows when it decides who can sell alcohol, put on live music, films or other entertainment, and serve hot food after 11pm. The policy does not decide individual applications, but it sets out what the council will take into account when it does.

questions.asked: People were asked for their views on a redrafted policy covering alcohol, entertainment and late-night food. The draft adds the 'agent of change' principle, so that developers building next to an existing pub or music venue deal with the noise rather than the venue; it adds commitments on the safety of women and girls and on staff getting home after late shifts; and, because of rising street drinking, the police and the council could ask shops applying to sell alcohol for drinking elsewhere to accept a condition on how strong the drink they sell can be. Sixty-seven responses to the survey came in before the consultation closed on 9 August 2026. What people actually said has not been published.
questions.decided: Two decisions so far. On 5 March 2026 the Licensing committee went through the draft, agreed a change to the wording on licence conditions, asked officers to look again at three further points — signage, logbook inspections and the paragraph numbering in one section — and recommended that Cabinet put the draft out to public consultation. It also asked Cabinet to consider further steps on the safety of women and girls during that consultation. Cabinet did both on 11 March 2026: it authorised the consultation and agreed to consider those further steps. Neither meeting decided the policy itself — after the consultation that goes to full council. The meeting where the responses are due, on 17 September 2026, had no papers published as of 7 September.
questions.done: Nothing yet. The policy Norwich applies today is still the one full council approved in December 2021: it took effect on 17 December 2021 and, in its own words, runs for no more than five years. Officers proposed taking a final version to full council in November 2026 so a new policy could start on 1 December 2026, before the current one expires. Until that happens, we are still waiting.

sources.title: Norwich's Licensing Policy — consultation (Get Talking Norwich)
sources.summary: The council's consultation page for the licensing policy review, open from 18 May to 9 August 2026 on its Get Talking Norwich site. It explains in plain terms what the policy covers — alcohol sales, live music, theatre and film, and hot food sold after 11pm — and that the law requires a review at least every five years. It promises that all responses will be analysed and summarised in a report to the Licensing committee in September 2026, with the final policy approved by full council. The survey is now closed and the page records 67 responses; the responses themselves are not published on it.

sources.title: Summary of changes to Licensing Policy.docx
sources.summary: A plain-English summary of what would change between the 2021 policy and the 2026 draft, written for residents rather than lawyers. It lists the main changes: aligning with the government's National Licensing Policy Framework of November 2025, formally adopting the 'agent of change' principle, a new commitment to work with the police and Norwich BID on a night-time safety charter, clearer rules on when conditions can be attached to a licence, a route for the council and the police to ask off-licences to accept a limit on high-strength alcohol, recognition of staff safety on late shifts, and published service standards. It stresses that most changes are clarifications rather than new rules, and that the four licensing objectives stay as they are.

sources.title: Draft Licensing Policy for consultation (full version)
sources.summary: The full draft policy residents were asked to comment on, 78 pages. sources.title: Draft Statement of Licensing Policy under the Licensing Act 2003
sources.summary: The officer's report to the 5 March 2026 committee, written by the council's Regulatory Services Manager. It explains that the Licensing Act 2003 requires a policy to be reviewed at least every five years, that the current one was adopted by full council in December 2021, and that a replacement has to be in place by December 2026 or licensing decisions could be open to challenge. It recommends sending the draft to Cabinet for public consultation, and sets out who must legally be consulted, including the chief constable, the fire service and Norfolk's director of public health. It also gives the scale of licensing in the city: 677 premises licences, 9 club premises certificates, 1,963 personal licences, and 225 temporary event notices — the short-notice permissions used for one-off events — during 2025.

sources.title: Appendix B - Summary of changes to 2021 statement of licensing policy
sources.summary: A table that goes through the policy paragraph by paragraph and says what is being added, deleted or reworded between the 2021 version and the 2026 draft. It is the quickest way to see the substance: new paragraphs on the agent of change principle, on tackling crime against women and other vulnerable people, on conditions restricting high-strength alcohol at off-licences, and on service standards; and the removal of the section on toilet facilities, now dealt with by other legislation. It also records two smaller changes people would notice in practice: control measures updated to allow military ID cards and digital ID where the law permits, and the removal of the requirement for public liability insurance. A good many of the entries are renumbering or tidying rather than a change of policy.

sources.title: Licensing policy approved by Norwich City Council, December 2021
sources.summary: The licensing policy that is actually in force in Norwich today, approved by full council in December 2021 and running to 79 pages. It sets out how the council decides applications to sell alcohol, put on regulated entertainment or serve hot food between 11pm and 5am, what conditions may be attached to a licence, and how licences are reviewed and enforced, with pools of model conditions for each of the four licensing objectives. It took effect on 17 December 2021 and, on its own terms, runs for no more than five years — which is why a replacement has to be in place by December 2026. The council publishes it as a PDF download.

events.title: Councillors agreed a draft policy and asked for it to go out to consultation
events.summary: On 5 March 2026 the Licensing committee went through a redrafted licensing policy. Officers asked for a change to the wording on licence conditions and members agreed it, then asked officers to look again at three further points during the consultation. They resolved to recommend the draft to Cabinet, to recommend that Cabinet start a 12-week public consultation, and to ask Cabinet to consider further steps on the safety of women and girls. This was a decision to ask the public, not a decision on the policy itself — that comes later, at full council.
detail: Paragraphs 7.1 and 7.4 were to change from 'necessary and proportionate' to 'appropriate and proportionate'. Officers said this gives the council more discretion when imposing conditions.

Officers were also asked to explore wording on making signage at premises easier to read, on how long premises must keep logbooks and who may inspect them, and to correct the paragraph numbering in section 3.

The committee formally asked Cabinet to consider further steps on the safety of women and girls during the consultation. A member had pressed for anti-spiking measures, door supervision and clearer ways for victims and staff to report problems.
The legal adviser noted that adopting the 'agent of change' principle was unusual for a licensing policy, though the national framework includes it.
The report proposed consulting from 11 May to 7 August 2026. It actually started a week later, on 18 May, and closed two days later than proposed, on 9 August.

gaps.description: What people said in the consultation. Sixty-seven responses were recorded, but neither the responses nor a summary of them has been published anywhere. The council's own commitment is that this appears in the report to the Licensing committee on 17 September 2026. Until then we can say what people were asked, not what they answered.

An explanation of one loose end. Councillors agreed on 5 March that paragraphs 7.1 and 7.4 should read 'appropriate and proportionate'. In the draft published for consultation on 18 May, both paragraphs still read 'necessary and proportionate'. We found no record saying whether the change was made later, dropped, or simply missed, so this needs checking with the council.

The Licensing committee also met on 8 June 2026, between the decision to consult and the meeting where results are due. That meeting's papers have not been checked, so we cannot say whether licensing policy came up at it.
The cumulative impact assessment. Officers told the March meeting one would be carried out separately from the policy and would run alongside the consultation. Nothing has been published.

The papers for the 17 September 2026 Licensing committee. As of 7 September 2026 the meeting page said there were no documents for it, so the officers' report on the consultation and any recommendation are not yet public.

Any record of the policy being used in an individual licensing decision. The draft policy says that where people object to an application, it has to be decided at a hearing of the council's Licensing sub-committee, and the council's premises licence page invites the public to comment on applications. We have not gathered any of those hearing records, so we cannot yet show the policy being applied case by case.

How many licence applications Norwich decides in a year, and how many it turns down. The officer's report to the March 2026 committee counts the licences in force but not the decisions behind them, and the council publishes no annual licensing report. We have not brought any national licensing statistics into the archive either, so no figures from elsewhere appear here.

The full Council meeting in December 2021 that adopted the current policy. The policy itself says it took effect on 17 December 2021, and the officer's report confirms Council adopted it that month, so the fact is well evidenced. We could not find the meeting record itself to link to.

A budget line for licensing on its own. Norwich's 2026-2027 General Fund budget is the most detailed money document the council publishes, and its service-by-service table stops at planning and regulatory services: licensing sits in there alongside planning, building control and the rest, budgeted together at £5.44m gross. So we can show the group's figures, never licensing's.

Licensing spending in the council's payments-over-£500 data. We read the January 2026 file line by line: 634 payments across 84 cost centres, and not one of them names licensing. The nearest thing is an expenditure category called “Planning & Regulatory Services GF Capital”, which covers the whole group. The dataset is published and complete; it simply is not cut in a way that shows what licensing buys.

Whether the fees licensing collects cover what the service costs to run. Fee levels for alcohol licensing are fixed in national regulations, so a council spending more than it takes in cannot simply charge more. Norwich publishes neither side of that sum for licensing on its own: not in the 2026-2027 budget, not in the fees book, and not in the payments-over-£500 data.
